# 10. Macros

<!-- Generated by tools/generate-docs.lisp from docs/manual/chapters.lisp,
     docs/manual/introduction.md and the examples: do not edit by hand. -->

Macros extend the language. syntax-rules macros are hygienic: their names
cannot capture a program's, nor be captured by them. define-macro macros work on
the forms directly.

## Hygienic macros

define-syntax with syntax-rules writes a macro as patterns and templates. The
macros are hygienic: a name a template binds cannot capture the program's
variables, and a name a template uses means what it meant where the macro was
defined, whatever the program has bound since. (define-macro is still there,
for macros that mean to capture.)

`examples/syntax-rules.lisp`:

```scheme
(define (show label x) (display label) (display " ") (write x) (newline))

;; swap! binds tmp. A program with its own tmp is safe from it.
(define-syntax swap!
  (syntax-rules ()
    ((_ a b) (let ((tmp a)) (set! a b) (set! b tmp)))))
(let ((tmp 'first) (other 'second))
  (swap! tmp other)
  (show "after (swap! tmp other):" (list tmp other)))

;; Patterns: literals, ellipses (repeated parts), nested ellipses.
(define-syntax my-cond
  (syntax-rules (else)
    ((_ (else e ...)) (begin e ...))
    ((_ (test e ...) clause ...) (if test (begin e ...) (my-cond clause ...)))))
(show "(my-cond (#f 1) ((= 1 1) 2) (else 3)) =" (my-cond (#f 1) ((= 1 1) 2) (else 3)))

(define-syntax my-let*
  (syntax-rules ()
    ((_ () body ...) (let () body ...))
    ((_ ((name value) more ...) body ...)
     (let ((name value)) (my-let* (more ...) body ...)))))
(show "my-let* =" (my-let* ((a 1) (b (+ a 1)) (c (* b 10))) (list a b c)))

(define-syntax table
  (syntax-rules ()
    ((_ (key value ...) ...) '((key value ...) ...))))
(show "table =" (table (fruit apple pear) (veg leek)))

;; A name the template uses keeps its meaning: here the program has bound list
;; and if locally, and the macro still means the global ones.
(define-syntax pair-up
  (syntax-rules () ((_ a b) (if #t (list a b) #f))))
(show "with local list and if:" (let ((list vector) (if 'not-a-keyword)) (pair-up 1 2)))

;; A special form's name is an ordinary name when the program binds it.
(show "((lambda (if) (if 1 2 3)) +) =" ((lambda (if) (if 1 2 3)) +))

;; let-syntax and letrec-syntax make local macros.
(show "letrec-syntax:"
      (letrec-syntax ((count-args (syntax-rules ()
                                    ((_) 0)
                                    ((_ x rest ...) (+ 1 (count-args rest ...))))))
        (count-args a b c d)))

;; syntax-error reports a misuse when the macro is expanded.
(define-syntax unary
  (syntax-rules ()
    ((_ x) (- x))
    ((_ x y ...) (syntax-error "unary takes one argument, not" x y ...))))
(show "(unary 5) =" (unary 5))
(show "(unary 1 2) is" (guard (e (#t (error-object-message e))) (eval '(unary 1 2))))
```

Its output:

```text
after (swap! tmp other): (second first)
(my-cond (#f 1) ((= 1 1) 2) (else 3)) = 2
my-let* = (1 2 20)
table = ((fruit apple pear) (veg leek))
with local list and if: (1 2)
((lambda (if) (if 1 2 3)) +) = 6
letrec-syntax: 4
(unary 5) = -5
(unary 1 2) is "unary takes one argument, not 1 2"
```

## A program's names are its own

Before Phase 9, two things went wrong: a local variable could not be named as
a special form, and the derived forms (case, cond, do, ...) used whatever
their helper names meant where they were used. Both are fixed: a binding
always wins over a special form's name, and the derived forms are hygienic
macros, whose names mean the global ones.

`examples/shadowing.lisp`:

```scheme
(define (show label x) (display label) (display " ") (write x) (newline))

;; A local named if is a variable like any other.
(show "((lambda (if) (if 1 2 3)) +) =" ((lambda (if) (if 1 2 3)) +))
(show "(let ((list vector)) (list 1 2)) =" (let ((list vector)) (list 1 2)))

;; case compares with the global memv, whatever memv means here.
(show "case with a local memv:"
      (let ((memv (lambda (key keys) #f)))
        (case 3 ((1 2 3) 'found) (else 'not-found))))

;; cond's expansion uses if, let and begin: local ones do not disturb it.
(show "cond with local if, let and begin:"
      (let ((if list) (let 1) (begin 2))
        (cond (#f 'first) ((> 2 1) 'second) (else 'third))))

;; do's loop has a name of its own, which a program's loop cannot be.
(show "do beside a variable named loop:"
      (let ((loop 'mine))
        (do ((i 0 (+ i 1)) (acc '() (cons i acc)))
            ((= i 3) (list acc loop)))))
```

Its output:

```text
((lambda (if) (if 1 2 3)) +) = 6
(let ((list vector)) (list 1 2)) = #(1 2)
case with a local memv: found
cond with local if, let and begin: second
do beside a variable named loop: ((2 1 0) mine)
```

## Extending the language with define-macro

`examples/macros.lisp`:

```scheme
; (while test body ...) -- a loop that cog-lisp does not have built in.
; The loop's own name comes from gensym, so it can never clash with a
; variable in the code the macro is used on.
(define-macro (while test . body)
  (let ((loop (gensym)))
    `(let ,loop ()
       (when ,test
         ,@body
         (,loop)))))

(define i 0)
(define total 0)
(while (< i 5)
  (set! total (+ total i))
  (set! i (+ i 1)))
(display "sum of 0..4 is ")
(display total)
(newline)

; a user variable named loop is not captured by the macro's loop
(define loop 3)
(while (> loop 0)
  (display loop)
  (display " ")
  (set! loop (- loop 1)))
(newline)

; macroexpand shows the code a macro call becomes
(display (macroexpand '(when (> x 0) (display x) x)))
(newline)

; quasiquote builds code and data alike
(define (make-adder-form n) `(lambda (x) (+ x ,n)))
(display (make-adder-form 10))
(newline)
(display ((eval (make-adder-form 10)) 5))
(newline)

; the derived forms are macros too, written in cog-lisp itself
(define (classify n)
  (cond ((< n 0) 'negative)
        ((= n 0) 'zero)
        (else (case (modulo n 2)
                ((0) 'even)
                (else 'odd)))))
(display (map classify '(-2 0 3 8)))
(newline)
```

Its output:

```text
sum of 0..4 is 10
3 2 1 
(if (> x 0) (begin (display x) x))
(lambda (x) (+ x 10))
15
(negative zero odd even)
```
